gholam.text:
ببین رفیق، تو دنیای پزشکی یه انقلاب بی‌سر‌و‌صدا به اسم siRNA راه افتاده که قراره کلاً قواعد بازی درمان رو عوض کنه. قدیما دانشمندا جون می‌کَندن تا با فرمول‌های شیمیایی جلوی پروتئین‌های بیماری‌زا رو سد کنن که خیلی وقتا نشدنی بود یا کلی عوارض داشت، اما این روش جدید مثل یه دکمه خاموش‌کن عمل می‌کنه و قبل از اینکه اصلاً پروتئین خرابکاری تو بدن تولید بشه، پیام ژنتیکیش رو ضربه‌فنی می‌کنه. الان داروهایی بر این اساس واسه درمان کلسترول بالا و بیماری‌های خونی سخت ساخته شده که مثل بارکدخوان با دقت بالا عمل می‌کنن و حتی یه دوز تزریقشون تا چند ماه تو بدن جواب می‌ده. فعلاً این درمان‌ها بیشتر رو کبد متمرکز شدن، ولی دانشمندا سخت دنبال اینن که با برچسب‌های مولکولی جدید، پای این تکنولوژی رو به تموم اندام‌های بدن باز کنن.

چرا مهمه؟ چون پروتئین‌های سرکشی که قبلاً هیچ دارویی حریفشون نمی‌شد و دست‌نیافتنی به حساب می‌اومدن، حالا به سادگی و بدون نیاز به دستکاری‌های پیچیده سلولی خنثی می‌شن.

links.text:
Most people have never heard of siRNA, but it’s going to change the face of medicine.
https://worksinprogress.co/issue/the-kill-switch-for-harmful-genes/

Much drug development today involves developing chemicals to fit into proteins and block them. But this almost never turns out as planned: many drug candidates get broken down in the body, interfere with other proteins and cause toxic side effects, or fail to be absorbed at all.

The majority of proteins are considered undruggable, because they lack a pocket for drugs to bind, or they are ‘intrinsically disordered’, without coherent structure.  

What if, instead of trying to block the protein, you could simply switch it off?

In a new article, Jacob Witten explains the magic button to silence genes. 

siRNA, or ‘small interfering RNA’, is a short strand of RNA that blocks the production of proteins. As a brief refresher, proteins in the body are produced through the sequence: DNA --> mRNA --> protein. siRNA molecules bind to the intermediate mRNA and target it for destruction, meaning the protein isn’t produced.

It’s a precision medicine: siRNA targets matching mRNA sequences like a barcode, so you can pick a gene of your choice, synthesize siRNA to match, deliver it to the right cells, and silence the protein. And a single dose can last months.

Several siRNA drugs have already been developed: patisiran for hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis, inclisiran for high cholesterol, and fitusiran for hemophilia, are just a few examples.

So far, all of them target the liver, which is an easy organ to deliver drugs to. But the principle can be applied to other organs too, and scientists are developing ‘molecular address labels’ to do it.

And while some of these diseases are caused by a single gene, not all are. High cholesterol, for example, is a complex disease, but it can be targeted with siRNA drugs as well, because the disease’s pathway hinges on a critical protein, PCSK9.

siRNA is exciting because it makes it possible to circumvent the problem of otherwise ‘undruggable’ proteins. And, unlike current gene-editing therapies, it can be given to people off the shelf, without needing to extract cells from the body, edit and replace them. But it’s still going to depend on having the right hypotheses of which genes to target and delivering the drugs safely to the right organs.

We now have a kill switch for harmful genes.

Read the full article here:
https://worksinprogress.co/issue/the-kill-switch-for-harmful-genes/
